"Madam, three of the Heron's Tithe's hands lie dead in our skiff, killed when they attacked us at the Gullspit light, and their master is a hooded man called Aldous, who sailed off with a man named Sparrow. DM: also, is there any word yet on whether Corvin has signed his statement and named the man he called "H."?

input.add_to_description: Day 9 evening, signed statement for Dame Crowe, held by the arbiter: Corvin names Elowen Ashgrove as his former teacher; says twenty years ago a man calling himself Aldous (grey cloak, a shipowner) paid him to find Elowen and her child and to 'bring the lamp-staff and the child'; Corvin took the money, found Elowen at Ashby Weir, did not harm her but took the child when Elowen fled, and raised her as his own apprentice, which he calls his worst and best act. Names 'H.' as Master Hale, Aldous's man who pressed Lord Edric and Osric; Sparrow is one of Hale's hands. Dates/places given: Lantern's Rest, Ashby Weir, Gullspit light. Wren has not yet read it in full.

Day 10 (from Corvin's statement): Hale is the man of 'Aldous', the Grey Cloak; Sparrow is one of Hale's hands. 'H.' in Corvin's note = Hale's watcher. Hale is held at Thornhallow for Dame Crowe's court.

Out of the story first. Yes, there's word on Corvin. The arbiter has it, and I'll give it to you as she reads it out below. He signed his statement at dusk last night, and it names "H."

Now the story. The arbiter takes in the three covered shapes in the skiff, Kit's grey face and your soaked cloak, and the white thread of the Gullspit light burning behind you. "Indoors," she says, "and by a fire." She sends Pell and his guards to carry the dead to the hall's cold room and has the hands looked at by someone who knows them. One of the Vantry porters mutters that they're Heron's Tithe men, regulars at the east quay.

In the elder's counting-room there's a good fire, bread, and a hot posset that Isaude Dray herself carries in and sets before you without a word. You give the arbiter your account in order: the Wick-House, Ysolde, the staff, Sparrow in the fog, the longboat, the Gullspit light, Brann, Elowen's grave, the squall. You leave nothing out except that you gave Brown the reliquary's foot to keep. She listens with her stylus still, which is the highest praise she gives.

Then she lays Corvin's statement before you, three closely written pages signed at the foot. She reads out the parts that matter. Corvin names Elowen Ashgrove as his own teacher. He says that twenty years ago a man calling himself Aldous, who wore a grey cloak and owned ships, paid him to find Elowen and her child and bring him "the lamp-staff and the child". Corvin took the money and found Elowen at Ashby Weir. She fled, and he took the child and raised her as his apprentice, which he calls "my worst act and my best." The "H." in his note is Master Hale, whom Aldous used to pressure Lord Edric and Osric and to watch the Wick-House. Sparrow is one of Hale's hands. The statement lists places and dates: Lantern's Rest, Ashby Weir, the Gullspit light. At the bottom, in Corvin's neat hand, is one more line: *I have not told her the rest. Let her ask me in person.*

The arbiter folds the pages carefully. "A copy goes to Dame Crowe at Marrowford," she says. "You have a seat at my fire as long as the weather keeps you, Mistress Ashgrove. After that, I would rather you were not on my quay when that grey sail returns."

It's seven past eleven. You have no spell slots, a day of aches, and a prisoner in the cellar with something he hasn't said. What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

Hale was paid and directed by a patron Corvin never met, who wrote in grey ink and signed his letters with a lantern drawn upside down. The patron first approached Corvin twenty years ago, asking where Elowen's blessings were hidden. Corvin signs *Corvin Tallowmere, storyteller and forger*, and underneath, in a smaller hand: *I did not know what she was to him.*

The arbiter folds the page. "This goes to Dame Crowe at Marrowford's assize, with your name beside it," she says. "I cannot hold a man for what he did sixteen years ago on a spit across the water, but I can see he is not loosed until she has had him." She considers you. "The Tithe's hands carried pikes marked with a heron. I will have the reeve ask who owns such a cutter. You may find the answer grows legs."

It is half past eleven. Your slots are empty, you're soaked and tired, and the Salt Gull has a bed. Corvin is in the cellar and the Wick-House is down the quay. What does Wren do?

entries.text: time: 1 hour 30 minutes later: Day 10, 11:27:12 AM

Out of the story first: yes. Corvin did sign. Pell reports it at the quay, and the arbiter confirms it a moment later. I'll give you the substance of it in the scene.

You step onto the wet stones, wring out your cloak, and meet the arbiter's eyes. You say it plainly: three hands of the Heron's Tithe lie dead in the skiff, killed when they attacked you at the Gullspit light, and their master is a hooded man named Aldous, who sailed off with Sparrow. The arbiter looks at the three shapes under their own cloaks for a long moment, at Kit, grey and soaked, and at the white thread of light across the water.

"Fire first," she says. "Then you talk."

She gives you the elder's counting-room again, with a fire, dry blankets, and a bowl of hot fish broth that you drink without tasting. The Vantry guards take the dead. Kit sits by the hearth with her sword across her knees and says nothing, with colour coming back into her face. Then you give it in full: the Wick-House, the staff, the strip of paper, Brann, the grave, the bandits, the grey sail. The arbiter writes without comment, and when you finish she sets her stylus down.

"Master Tallowmere signed at dawn," she says. "I witnessed and sealed it myself." She slides a copy across the table to you. In his neat hand, it says that he was Elowen Ashgrove's apprentice and sold her blessings for coin. He found the coffer but never her, and he names the man he called "H." as Master Hale. Hale, he says, is the hand of a grey-cloaked patron called Aldous, once of the Lantern-Bearer's own order, who has hunted Elowen's three hidden bequests for sixteen years. Corvin did not know his sailing port. He asks, at the bottom, to be heard by Dame Crowe and by "my apprentice, if she will."

It is past eleven. Hale is already in a cell at Thornhallow. The patron he served is out on the water, and the white light on the spit has stopped half the town working. You've spells to recover, a lamp to keep burning, and a hearing at Marrowford at month's end.

What does Wren do?

entries.text:
You wring out your cloak on the quay and give the arbiter your account in as few words as will carry it: three dead hands, the Gullspit light, a hooded man called Aldous, and Sparrow. She looks at the shapes in the skiff, then at the white thread of light on the estuary, and her mouth tightens.

"By a fire," she says. "Pell, take the dead to the hall cellar and have the dockmaster look at them. Mistress, with me."

In the counting-room off the hall, a brazier throws heat and the squall rattles the shutters. Kit stands dripping at the door, and you tell it all, with the strip from the staff on the table, in order. The arbiter listens, her stylus still, and Pell comes in once to say the dockmaster knows two of the dead men. They are Saltmarsh dockhands, hired for coin by the cutter's master three days ago, whose names they didn't know.

Then she reads you Corvin's statement, signed in the night before the clerk and the cellar guard. It is long and plain. In it he names "H." as Master Hale, and says Hale and Sparrow serve a patron he knows only as Aldous. This patron paid him in sea-coin for sixteen years to forge noble pedigrees and to sell Elowen's blessings, and wants her lamp-staff and the lamp. Corvin writes that he kept you away from Aldous by raising you himself, and that he let the ledger be "stolen" to bring you here. The towns and dates for Elowen are there too, and they match what Brann told you.

Whether any of it is true, you can't say. It reads honest enough that a stranger would believe it. Corvin always did write well.

"I will send this to Dame Crowe at Marrowford with a clerk's seal," the arbiter says. "She'll want you at the assize by month's end. She'll want Corvin too." She sets down the paper and looks at you as one looks at a candle that has been burning a long time. "You need a bed. Sleep, then decide what you are going to do about a man named Aldous."

It is nearly noon. You have no spell slots, one use of Bardic Inspiration, a sore body, and the Salt Gull's room. What does Wren do?

sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 12 ~12:33 AM: shot Wren twice (10 damage), then surrendered at 4 HP, lit in violet Faerie Fire, hand crossbow dropped. A scout (hired spy) in a brown cloak, lean, no smile. Prisoner at the Rushlight House yard. Not yet questioned.

entries.text:
You drop below the sill, breathe the Lantern-Bearer's word across your own ribs, and the bolt-sting eases. You heal 7 and are back to 14 of 17, with one slot left. You pop up again and snap your insult across the yard, with the road's own bite in it: "You're bleeding, friend, and the horse is farther than the hook!" He shrugs it off with a natural 20, so the mockery does nothing.

But he is a professional, and he can count. He's lit like a lantern on a dark shore with a bolt in his ribs and another through his sleeve. Kit's crossbow is trained on his chest, Tamsin's hook has come out of the shadow of the ferry shed, and the nearest cover is twenty paces off. On his turn he lets his hand crossbow fall into the shingle, raises both hands, and says in a flat, tired voice that isn't Sparrow's:

"I yield. Don't shoot again."

The fight ends there, with three rounds, eighteen seconds, and 100 XP for the scout (475 of 900). Faerie Fire still outlines him in violet. Kit steps out of the byre with the crossbow level and her shield on her arm. Tamsin, hook raised, circles behind him. Annis's cracked voice calls from inside: "Is it over? The cat's settled."

He is lean, not smiling, and rather young under the hood. He has a bandage's worth of blood on his sleeve and a brown cloak, and his horse is somewhere beyond the dike. It's half past midnight, and you have a prisoner, a sleeping village, and a long night before dawn. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 12 ~12:33 AM: wounded to 4 HP in the yard at Reedlow by Kit's crossbow after Wren's Faerie Fire; surrendered to Wren's Intimidation (21). Now a prisoner at the Rushlight House. He is a lean, hard-faced young man, NOT Sparrow; he gives the name Dace (may be false). Carried a hand crossbow, a shortsword and a wax-sealed slip not yet read.

entries.text:
You drop below the sill, breathe the Lantern-Bearer's word, and the sting in your ribs eases. That's 5 healed, so you're at 12 of 17, with one slot left. Then you pop up and snap another insult at him, and he shrugs that off too. You call the rest across the yard in your gruffest fishwife voice: "Surrender now, and you'll leave with a bandage and your life. Run, and Kit shoots you in the back."

Your Intimidation is a 21. He looks at the violet light on his own hands, at the byre door where Kit's crossbow follows him, and at the thirty feet of open shingle between him and the dike. Then he lets the hand crossbow slip from his fingers into the mud and raises both hands.

"All right," he says, in a flat, young voice. "All right. I've had enough."

Kit comes out of the byre with her sword up and kicks the crossbow away. Tamsin, hook in one hand and rope in the other, ties his wrists with a ferryman's knots that look a lot better than any you've seen. You open the door. He is a lean, hard-faced young man, no older than twenty-five, with a bloody sleeve and the sullen look of someone who has run out of luck. He gives his name as Dace. He is not Sparrow, and you have no reason to believe the name. In his belt is a shortsword and a small wax-sealed slip of paper that you haven't read.

Faerie Fire gutters out. You get 100 XP for him, so you are at 475 of 900. Annis calls drily from behind the hearth, "Is it done? The cat's gone quiet." It is nearly a quarter to one in the morning. Tamsin stands over the prisoner with her hook, and Kit watches the dike road. What does Wren do?

You drop below the sill, whisper Healing Word into your own ribs, and feel the ache close a little. It heals 5, and you're at 12 of 17. Then you come back up and snap your mockery through the gap: "You're bleeding, friend, and the horse is farther than the hook!" He fails his save, takes 1, and flinches as the insult lands. His next attack would suffer for it.

It doesn't matter. He looks at the violet glow he can't shake off, at the dark byre where Kit's crossbow is already wound, and at the thirty open feet between him and the dike.
